rows.text: This looks straightforward enough that my team wouldn't need training for the basic sign-in and workspace creation — the fields are labeled plainly, the password rules give live feedback, and the CRO-versus-own-company choice maps directly to how I actually work. The MFA setup and reset flows read as conventional, so I'd expect low friction. My only mild irritation is the demo-code reveal button, but I understand that's a sandbox artifact.

Honestly, this is a sign-in and account page — it's about as easy as any of the auth screens my team logs into daily, so I'd have no trouble. The disabled-until-filled button, Enter-to-submit, and the live password rule counter are all the small courtesies I expect. The CRO-vs-own-company fork at signup is a nice touch since I file on behalf of clients, and it puts the right label in front of me without making me think.

The three-column layout with a numbered journey rail, a live readiness panel and locked steps that tell me *why* they're locked is genuinely more navigable than clicking through docuBridge sections blind, so I could see myself moving through it. That said, ten sequential steps with gating is a lot for someone who files non-linearly the way my team does, and I'd want to know I can jump around without the tool fighting me. The "Check my pathway" routing and auto-save lower the barrier for a junior associate, which matters to me since I'm buying for nine people, not just myself.

Honestly this looks manageable — the numbered left rail with "you're here," locks with reasons, and a clear "Continue" path is more hand-holding than Vault or docuBridge give you, so a junior on my team could follow it. My worry is the opposite: it's very wizard-driven, and experienced people like me who work non-linearly (jumping between Module 1 labelling and Module 3 while waiting on data) may feel boxed in by the locked steps. The three-column layout is a lot on screen, but nothing here looks hard to operate.

This looks straightforward to navigate, honestly more approachable than docuBridge for someone new. The New dossier flow is a simple inline form and the ID-format hint plus the placeholder-ID escape hatch mean I wouldn't get stuck waiting on a real Dossier ID to start work. My only friction is the volume of chips and toggles on the home page, but nothing here would intimidate my team.

This looks straightforward enough for me and my team - it maps onto the RIM mental model I already carry, so creating a dossier, filtering, and archiving would take no real training. I appreciate that the "New dossier" form is inline and short rather than a ten-field wizard. The one friction point is the required Dossier ID at creation; realistically we often don't have the real Health Canada ID yet, so I'd lean on that placeholder path constantly and would want to be sure the "set real ID" step is hard to forget.

Honestly, the three-column layout is close to how my team already works in Vault, so I could find my way around, but there's a lot packed into that center panel — mode toggles, expanders, teach boxes, review panels — and I'd want to know it doesn't overwhelm a junior associate. The "Author in-app" path with pre-filled known facts and greyed example text is a sensible pattern; that would genuinely save clicks versus building leaves by hand in docuBridge.

The three-column layout is familiar territory for anyone who has lived in Vault or docuBridge, so my team would orient quickly, and I like that the tree, the section detail, and the readiness card are all visible at once. What worries me is the sheer density on one screen — badges, tooltips, expanders, buckets, toggles — and for AI-eligible sections the extra mode toggle adds a decision point. A junior associate could get lost between "Upload," "Author in-app," and the AI path without training.

Honestly this reads as fairly straightforward — three clear ways to complete a section, and the chat drafting is the sort of thing my junior staff would pick up quickly. What I'd worry about is my team treating "Draft with AI" as the path of least resistance and rushing through. The two-step gate (use draft, then attest) adds clicks, but I'd want those clicks, so I don't mind the friction.

The flow is reasonably linear — pick "Author in-app", chat, "Use this draft", then confirm — and I appreciate that the gates are hard to miss. But there are a lot of stacked toggles (Upload/Author/N/A, then Draft-with-AI/Fill-the-form) and the chat-to-draft-to-confirm sequence is more clicks than my team is used to in Vault. For a junior associate it would take a walkthrough or two before it's muscle memory.

Honestly this looks manageable for me — the flow is roughly what I already do mentally: run a check, look at findings by rule id, then export a sequence. The layered disclosures (rule catalogue, "what this does/does NOT check") are the kind of thing I'd click once and then ignore, which is fine. My only friction is the sheer number of small controls scattered across three surfaces (completeness card, Application Viewer, Sequences), so I'd need to learn where each lever lives before I'd trust my nine analysts not to miss one.

Honestly this looks manageable — the completeness card, the findings list with error/warning chips, and the export-blocked-until-you-fix flow all map to how I already think. The truncation to 5 errors and 3 warnings with a "Show all" toggle is sensible for a quick scan. My team could pick this up without much hand-holding, though the override-with-typed-reason step will need a documented SOP so people don't abuse it.

For someone who lives in Vault RIM and docuBridge, the layout reads familiar enough — a portfolio grid, per-row expanders, register/correspondence/audit tabs. My concern is the density: the row packs submission type, module tower, status chip, fee, litigation clocks and collaboration chips behind a "Details" expander, and I'd want to see how much clicking my team does to work a real portfolio. But nothing here looks like it would defeat a regulatory associate.

The layout is dense but logical, and I recognize the shape of it — portfolio, registry, correspondence, audit are the four things my team lives in. What I appreciate is that the primary status chip is a single answer per row with the messier details tucked into an expander, which is how I'd want my nine people to scan a book of business. The one worry is training my juniors on the DSTS lifecycle and NOA-clock language, which isn't self-evident from the row itself.

The three-column layout with a step rail, an active card, and a persistent readiness tower is a sensible shape, and a live percent-ready chip in the top bar is the kind of at-a-glance signal I actually want. I'd want to see it under load with a real dossier, but on paper the navigation reads as approachable for my team, which is what matters when I'm rolling this out to nine people of varying comfort.

Honestly this looks straightforward — it's a standard email/password sign-in with the usual guardrails: disabled button until fields are filled, Enter-to-submit, a live password-rule counter. Nothing here would slow me down, and the CRO-vs-own-company fork at signup is a nice touch since I've filed both ways. The MFA and reset flows behave the way I'd expect from any modern tool.

Honestly this looks about as frictionless as auth gets — labeled fields, Enter-to-submit, disabled button until both fields are filled, live password rules. I'd be in and set up in under a minute, and the MFA and reset flows read like something I've done a hundred times in eCTD Office. Nothing here would slow me down.

The three-column layout with a numbered rail, active card, and readiness panel is legible, and I like that later steps are locked with a plain reason rather than just greyed out. The "Check my pathway" routing helper and dashed-underline term definitions would let me move fast without hunting through guidance PDFs. My worry is the sheer length — ten steps end to end — but since progress saves automatically and I can revisit unlocked steps, that's manageable for someone who does this daily.

Honestly this reads like it'd be easy enough for me to move through — the numbered rail with locked/unlocked steps and a "you're here" marker is basically how I already think about a sequence. My worry is that ten guided steps might feel slow when I'm doing this fifteen times a year and just want to get to document assembly and validation. If unlocked steps are freely revisitable I can live with it, but I'd want a way to skip the hand-holding once I know the drill.

This looks straightforward for me — it's the same mental model as the dossier folders I keep in SharePoint, just cleaner. Grid/list toggle, filter by ID or product, sortable columns with soonest-due flagging is exactly how I'd triage 15 sequences a year. The inline create card with a placeholder-ID option means I'm not blocked waiting on the real ID, which is realistic.

Honestly this looks manageable for someone like me who lives in eCTD Office and GlobalSubmit daily. The three-column layout with a section tree, a work panel, and a transmit-readiness column maps to how I already think, and the Upload/Author/Mark-N/A toggle is exactly the decision I make per leaf. The one thing that would slow me down is the volume of expanders and tooltips packed in — for a power user that's a lot of clicking to reach things I'd want visible by default.

Honestly this reads like it'd be easy for someone like me to navigate — portfolio, registry, correspondence, audit are the right buckets and the layout is sensible. The one primary status chip per row with a Details expander is a good call; I don't want fifteen chips screaming at me. My only friction is the correspondence page stacking three panels behind a "pick a dossier" gate — I'd want to see how that feels with 40 active sequences, not one.

Honestly this looks well organized to someone who lives in dossier assembly — portfolio, registry, correspondence, audit are the four buckets I actually work in, and the at-a-glance gate/fee/module status is how my brain already sorts sequences. The per-row "Details" expander and the CSV exports are sensible. My only friction is the sheer density; there's a lot stacked on one page and I'd want to see whether the mini module tower maps cleanly to the eCTD granularity I file, but nothing here reads as hard to operate.

The three-column layout — step rail, active card, submission tower with a readiness chip — is exactly how my head already works when I assemble a sequence, so I'd be productive fast. The plain-language-but-precise framing plus hover definitions means I wouldn't have to babysit junior staff through it. My only friction is I can't tell how much manual assembly it saves versus eCTD Office; a walkthrough reads easy, real granule-level work rarely is.

The nav is clean and I'd find my way around fast, high tech comfort here. Pulling the rule catalogue live from the engine and grouping it into expandable families is genuinely how I'd want to browse validation rules, not hunt through a PDF. The three-column layout with the submission tower and a readiness percentage reads like something I could operate without training.

Honestly this looks straightforward to get into — it's just an email and password sign-in, the button won't let me submit until both fields are filled, and Enter works, which is how I'd expect it. The signup even asks "Your own company" vs "on behalf of clients (CRO)," and since I'm at a CRO that mapping is nice and obvious. The MFA and reset flows have plain helper text, so I don't think I'd get stuck.

Honestly this looks pretty approachable for someone at my level — the numbered journey rail with a "You're here" marker and locked steps that tell you why they're locked is exactly the hand-holding I need, because right now I'm just guessing which order to do things in from a Word template. The three-column layout might feel busy at first, but having the step card in the middle and readiness on the right seems manageable. My only worry is the "Check my pathway" routing thing — I'd want to be sure I'm picking the right filing type, because I still mix up ANDS vs SNDS.

Honestly this looks pretty approachable for someone like me. The left rail with "You're here," done checks, and locked steps that tell you WHY they're locked would keep me from getting lost, which is my biggest fear right now doing this off Word templates. The one worry is the sheer number of steps and fields on that first "Tell me about your drug" panel — I'd still probably need a senior to confirm I picked the right pathway before I trusted the "Check my pathway" verdict.

Honestly this looks manageable — it's a lot like organizing files, and the "New dossier +" card walks me through the fields one at a time. I appreciate that the ID field shows me the format up front and flags an invalid ID before I get too far. The one thing that would slow me down is knowing which submission type to pick and whether the "Comparative-BE only / CS-BE path" checkbox applies to my product, since that's exactly the kind of call I still ask a senior about.

Honestly this looks fairly approachable for me. Creating a dossier is basically filling out a short form, and I like that there's a "start with a placeholder" option because on my first filings I won't have the real Dossier ID from Health Canada yet. The filter, "just my dossiers" checkbox, and grid/list toggle all feel familiar from other web tools I use.

Honestly this looks like a lot to take in on a first pass. Three columns with a tree, a form panel, and a transmit panel is a bit dense, but the toggle buttons (Upload / Author in-app / Mark N/A) and the drop zones are the kind of thing I'd figure out. What actually reassures me is the "example - replace this" greyed text and the pre-filled known facts, because half my job is not forgetting a field.

Honestly this looks like a lot to take in at once, three columns with tons of little icons, badges, expanders and tooltips. But the fact that each section tells me if it's Required or Optional and shows a progress bar and an "X/Y required placed" count would help me a lot, since right now I'm just cross-checking a Word template against the guidance by hand. I'd need someone to walk me through it once, but after that the upload-or-author-in-app choice seems simple enough.

Honestly this looks pretty approachable for someone like me — it's basically a chat box, and the placeholder even shows me the kind of thing to type, so I wouldn't feel lost. I like that it says the AI will ask me for details instead of leaving blanks, because right now I never know what a section actually wants. The three buttons (Upload, Author in-app, Mark N/A) are self-explanatory, and I don't have to figure out a template on my own unless I want to.

Honestly this looks pretty approachable for me since I basically live in chat now. I pick "Author in-app," then "Draft with AI," type what I know about the sponsor, and it asks me for the rest instead of leaving me staring at blank fields, which is exactly the kind of hand-holding I need at 1.5 years in. The two-step toggle (Upload / Author / Mark N/A, then Draft vs Fill the form) is one click more than I'd expect but it's not confusing.

Honestly it looks manageable — the completeness card, findings list, and export chip all seem to sit where I'd expect, and the "Show all N findings" toggle means I'm not drowning in a wall of errors right away. What worries me is the number of moving parts: completeness check, Application Viewer, Sequences card, override panels — I'd need someone senior to walk me through which one to actually click first for my ANDS. The typed-reason override and "make active" sequence stuff feels like something I could fumble on my first real filing.

Honestly, this looks like a lot of chips, expanders and toggles all on one screen, and I'd be nervous clicking around at first. But the fact that export just runs the check for me and downloads a zip is nice — I don't have to remember the steps. The "Export blocked" flow that names the issue count and tells me to go fix the module pages is exactly the kind of hand-holding I need right now.

Honestly it seems mostly readable to me — the Portfolio page with the three summary cards, the deadline warning, and the "Open →" link feels like something I could pick up. But there's a LOT crammed in here: registry, correspondence, notice inbox, NOA register, audit trail. As someone still learning, I'd be nervous about knowing which page I'm supposed to be on for a given task, and I'd probably have to click around a fair bit before it clicked.

Honestly this looks like a lot to take in — Portfolio, Registry, Correspondence, Audit, each with their own sub-panels and forms. The Portfolio row itself seems manageable, but the Correspondence page with three stacked panels and the DSTS lifecycle stuff feels like something I'd need a senior to walk me through the first time. The per-DIN deadline cards and the "Details" expander are nice because they hide complexity until I ask for it.

Honestly this looks approachable for someone at my level. The "Start my submission" button and the step rail on the left tell me exactly where to begin, and the readiness percentage in the top bar means I'm not guessing whether I've missed something. The three-column layout with the module tower on the right is a lot to take in at once, but nothing here feels like it would trip me up on day one.

Honestly this looks approachable for someone like me. The "Start my submission" button and the step-by-step journey rail mean I'm not staring at a blank Word template wondering where to begin, and having a readiness percentage in the top bar tells me at a glance how far off I am. My only worry is whether the three-column layout gets overwhelming once real data fills it in, but on paper it seems easy enough to find my footing.

Honestly this reads as straightforward for me — labeled Email and Password fields, a button that stays greyed out until I fill both, Enter-to-submit. The password rules count down as you type, which is the kind of hand-holding I'd want. The reset flow with a "Reveal demo code" button is a bit of a head-scratcher on first read, but they flag it's demo-only, so I'd manage.

Honestly this looks straightforward enough for me to get into — filled fields, a disabled button until I'm done, Enter-to-submit, that's all standard and I wouldn't need hand-holding. The password rules counting down as you type and the plain "New here? Create a workspace" wording are the kind of thing that keeps me from fumbling. My only friction is the MFA authenticator-app step, which I'd want IT to walk me through the first time, but that's on me, not the tool.

The three-column layout with a numbered rail, a "You're here" marker, and locked steps that explain why they're locked feels manageable, even for someone like me who avoids fiddly software. What I can't judge from a written walkthrough is how much data entry sits behind each of those ten steps, and my worry is that the friendly framing hides a lot of grinding underneath. The auto-save is welcome, though I'd want to know where that saved session actually lives.

The three-column layout with a numbered rail, a step card, and a readiness panel is about as approachable as I could hope for something this involved — the locked steps with a plain reason for why they're closed is exactly how I'd want a junior to be walked through it. My worry is the sheer number of moving parts on one screen; at my comfort level a 3D "submission tower" is noise I'd toggle straight to the printable checklist. But overall, for a cautious person, being unable to skip ahead and being told where I am reduces the chance I make a mess.

Honestly this looks manageable for someone like me — the create form is a plain set of fields and the buttons say what they do. What I appreciate is that I'm not forced to invent a Dossier ID; the placeholder option and the format hint mean I won't get stuck the first time I try. The delete flow asks me to type the ID and a reason, which is more friction, but that's the good kind of friction in my world.

Honestly, this looks more approachable than I expected. Creating a dossier is a plain form with sensible placeholders, and the grid/list toggle plus a filter box is the kind of thing I already do in our document vault. My worry is the sheer number of new terms thrown at me on one screen, but the flow itself seems clickable without training.

Honestly, that's a lot of columns and controls to take in on one screen, and I'd need to sit with it before I trusted my own hands on it. That said, the three-column layout is logical and the "Upload / Author in-app / Mark N/A" choices map to how I actually think about assembling a section. The plain-language eCTD primer and the "What Health Canada needs here" box would genuinely help someone on my team who doesn't live in the guidance every day.

Honestly it looks busy — three columns with trees, buckets, expanders and toggles is a lot to take in, and I'd want a half-day of training before I trusted myself in it. That said, the fact that each section tells me plainly "Required" or "Optional" and shows a progress bar and a "needed to file" count is the kind of structure I work well with. My worry is less the individual controls and more remembering where everything lives across all those collapsed panels.

Honestly, the mechanics look manageable — pick "Author in-app," chat with the assistant, click "Use this draft," then confirm. But I don't assemble these sections myself; I review what others hand me, and I'd worry my staff would rush through the chat step. The multiple nested toggles (Upload/Author/N-A, then Draft-with-AI/Fill-the-form) are a bit of a maze for someone who just wants to fill in a form.

Honestly, this reads like something I could follow without much hand-holding, which surprised me for an AI feature. The three choices up front — Upload, Author in-app, Mark N/A — are plain language, and the fact that nothing saves until I click "Use this draft" means I can poke around without breaking anything. My worry is the chat itself: I'm not fast at typing prompts, and "tell it about the submission" is vague enough that I'd stall wondering how much detail it actually wants.

Honestly, this looks reasonably approachable for someone in my seat, because it reads more like a checklist than a black box. I'd be clicking through the "What this does / does NOT check" and the rule catalogue before I trusted a single finding, and I appreciate that both are one click away. The override-with-typed-reason step is exactly the kind of deliberate friction I'd expect, so I wouldn't feel rushed into anything.

The one thing that would slow me down is knowing which of these views is my system of record when they overlap.

Reading through it, I think I could follow the basic loop — run the completeness check, look at the findings, then export. The concepts map onto what I already do with submission QC, so the layout doesn't intimidate me. What I'm less sure about is the sequences and lifecycle-operator side; "2× new, 1× replace" and making a sequence active is more moving parts than I'd want to get right on my first pass without someone walking me through it.

Honestly, this looks like a lot to take in on a single set of screens, but the structure follows how I already think — portfolio, registry, correspondence, audit. The append-only audit trail with actor, timestamp, and sequence numbers is exactly the mental model I use, so navigating it wouldn't fight me. My worry is the density: mini module towers, status chips, litigation clocks, fee chips buried in a "Details" expander — I'd need a walkthrough before I trusted myself to read a row correctly.

Reading it, I can follow the layout well enough — cards, rows, a Details expander, separate pages for Registry, Correspondence and Audit. But there's a lot packed in, and someone at my comfort level would need a proper SOP and a walkthrough before touching it live. The per-row status chip and the mini module tower are the kind of at-a-glance view I actually want when I'm signing off, so the everyday scanning would be manageable.

The three-column layout with a step rail, a middle card, and a readiness panel sounds orderly, and I appreciate that it resumes a saved session rather than making me start over. My worry is the sheer number of concepts thrown at me on the landing page alone, but the guided step-by-step framing and plain-language explanations would lower the barrier for someone at my comfort level.

Reading it, the flow seems sensible enough — a step rail, a card in the middle, a readiness panel — but I've been burned by tools that look tidy in a walkthrough and turn into a maze once you're three modules deep. The "readiness percentage" and "start over" button are the kind of thing my staff could follow, so I'd rate this as moderately approachable, not effortless. I'd need to sit with it hands-on before I'd say more.

This looks straightforward to get into — a single card, labeled Email and Password fields, a button that sensibly stays disabled until I've filled both, and Enter-to-submit. The CRO path matters to me since I file on behalf of six-plus clients, and I like that choosing "On behalf of clients" reworks the labels to "Client company name." Nothing here would slow me down.

Honestly this looks straightforward to get into — labeled fields, a disabled button until both are filled, Enter-to-submit, and clear helper text on passwords and MFA codes. The CRO branch ("On behalf of clients") mapping to a client company name is exactly how I think about my six sponsors, so I wouldn't fumble it. Nothing here would slow me down.

The locked-step rail with plain-language reasons and a "Check my pathway" verdict is the kind of hand-holding my less-experienced clients would appreciate, so navigating it looks straightforward. For me personally it might feel a bit slow — I already know I'm filing an ANDS, and I'd want to skip the teaching paragraphs and get to the assembly and validation. Overall it reads as easy to pick up.

The locked-step rail with plain-language reasons and a "you're here" marker is genuinely how I mentally walk clients through a filing, so I'd find it easy to follow. The one worry is the "Check my pathway" panel — if it silently mis-routes a SANDS as an ANDS, "easy" becomes dangerous. Saved progress and a single named blocker are the kind of thing that would save me repeated hand-holding emails.

Honestly this reads as fairly easy to navigate — it's a familiar dossier-list-and-create pattern, and the inline "New dossier" card asks for exactly the fields I'd expect (Dossier ID, product, submission type). What I appreciate is that the friction is in the right places: the typed-ID-plus-reason confirmation to delete is exactly the deliberate speed-bump I want, not an annoyance.

This sits close to how I already work, so it wouldn't be a heavy lift for me. The New dossier form has the fields I'd expect, the placeholder-ID path is a sensible touch for clients who haven't filed the Dossier ID Request yet, and I appreciate that delete asks for a typed ID plus a reason. My only friction is the number of chips and toggles crowding the top; I'd want to see it live before judging whether it's genuinely quick.

Honestly, this looks dense — three columns with trees, expanders, toggles, buckets, and a 3D "tower." I'd manage, because I know eCTD structure cold and the leaf/sequence/operator vocabulary is my daily bread, but a junior at a sponsor client would drown in it. The one thing that saves it is the progress bar and "X/Y required placed" count, which is exactly how I mentally track a Module 1 completeness pass.

Honestly, the three-column layout with a section tree on the left, the working section in the middle, and a transmit-readiness card on the right maps to how I already think when I screen an ANDS, so I'd find my way around quickly. The status icons, N/A buckets, and per-section "Required/Optional" line are close to my own checklists. My only worry is the sheer density on one screen — for a client's assistant who doesn't live in eCTD, that's a lot to absorb at once.

Honestly this reads as straightforward — pick "Author in-app," chat with the assistant, click "Use this draft," then click the attestation button. The flow is linear and the buttons say what they do. My only friction is that chatting my way to a regulatory document feels slower and less controllable than filling a structured form, so I'd probably gravitate to the "Fill the form" tab for anything I know cold.

Reasonably easy — the Upload / Author / Mark N/A split fits how I triage, and a chat that asks for missing details beats blank templates. It's a few more gated clicks than my Word workflow, but each gate is justified.

The layout reads logically enough — a completeness card, a findings list, a viewer, and sequences — but there's a lot packed in, and I'd want to click around before I trusted my read of it. The truncation to first-5-errors and first-3-warnings with a "Show all" toggle worries me; when I screen I want every finding on one page, not paged. The typed-reason override gate is familiar territory and I'd manage it fine.

If the walkthrough matches reality, this would be workable for me — the status chip, findings rows, and the export-blocks-on-check flow map cleanly onto how I already think. My one friction is the sheer number of surfaces (completeness card, Application Viewer, Sequences panel) that all touch validation; I'd need a pass or two to learn where each control lives, especially the override buried in the Sequences panel rather than next to the export button.

On paper this reads like something I could sit down with. The pages are laid out the way I actually think about a portfolio — dossier, status, fee, deadline — and the forms ask for the fields I'd expect. My worry is the density: three stacked panels on Correspondence and all those chips per row is a lot to absorb, and I can't judge real ease until I've clicked through it myself.

The layout follows a logic I already work in — portfolio at a glance, then registry, correspondence, audit — so I could find my way without much hand-holding. But there's a lot packed behind expanders and stacked panels, and I'd need to click through every "Details" to see fee and litigation-clock status, which slows down the client-status sweeps I do weekly. The DIN field with live 8-digit validation and the "leave blank until NOC" hint is exactly the kind of small courtesy that saves me correcting a client's sponsor later.

Reading it, the shape is familiar enough that I could find my way — a top nav, a start button, a three-column workspace with a step rail and a module tower. I appreciate that it resumes a saved session, because half my frustration with tools is losing my place. The "submission tower" and "readiness percentage" are new vocabulary to me but I'd pick them up quickly.

On paper the navigation reads cleanly, and the three-column layout with a step rail and a readiness chip is roughly how my brain already organizes a submission, so I'd expect to find my way around without much training. What I can't judge from a walkthrough is whether the day-to-day of actually assembling Module 1 and the two Product Monographs is as smooth as the marketing copy, but the structure itself doesn't intimidate me.

Honestly this looks easy — it's a standard sign-in/signup card, and as a CRO-vs-own-company choice up front it clearly speaks to how I'd actually set up. The password rules, live character countdown, and Enter-to-submit are the small things that make me not fight the form. Nothing here would slow me or my team down.

Honestly this looks dead simple to get into — it's a plain sign-in card, and the "Who are you filing for?" fork between "your own company" and "on behalf of clients (CRO)" tells me right away it's built for someone like me, not just consultancies. Password rules count down live, Enter submits, buttons disable until filled — that's the polish I expect from Notion or any modern SaaS. I wouldn't need a manual to create a workspace.

Honestly, this looks navigable for someone like me who's comfortable with tools but knows nothing about filings — the numbered journey rail, locked steps with plain reasons, and auto-save are exactly the guardrails I'd need. What worries me is the sheer number of steps (10) and the alphabet soup of "NDS, SANDS, SNDS, DIN" hitting me right at step 1; I'd want the tool to just tell me which one I am, not make me pick. The dashed-underline hover definitions are a nice touch that would keep me from constantly Googling.

Honestly this looks pretty usable for someone like me who's comfortable with software but knows nothing about regulatory. The three-column layout with a numbered rail, an active step card, and a live readiness tracker is the kind of guided flow I'd expect from a good SaaS product, and locked steps with a plain reason beats being dumped into a blank form. My one worry is the sheer number of steps (10) and unfamiliar fields, but the "you're here" and auto-save mean I could stop and come back without losing my place.

Honestly this looks manageable for someone like me who lives in Notion all day. The New dossier flow is a normal form, the grid/list toggle and filter bar are patterns I already know, and the placeholder-ID trick means I'm not blocked waiting on Health Canada to even start poking around. The type-the-ID-plus-reason to archive is a couple extra steps, but I get why it's there.
